content: Fluvoxamine is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) that has been approved for the treatment of depression, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and various anxiety disorders. It is available in an oral formulation. Although fluvoxamine has not been approved for the treatment of infections, it has been used in the early management of individuals with mild to moderate COVID-19. Given the limited number of effective therapies for COVID-19 in community settings, it is important to thoroughly evaluate the current evidence regarding the efficacy and safety of fluvoxamine as a potential anti-inflammatory and antiviral treatment for COVID-19. This evaluation is based on data from randomized controlled trials (RCTs). The objective of this review was to assess the efficacy and safety of fluvoxamine when added to standard care, compared to standard care alone (with or without placebo) or any other pharmacological treatment with proven efficacy, in both outpatient and inpatient settings for individuals with COVID-19. To identify relevant studies, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane COVID-19 Study Register, MEDLINE, Embase, ClinicalTrials.gov, WHO ICTRP, medRxiv, Web of Science, and the WHO COVID-19 Global Literature database. The search included completed and ongoing studies up to February 1, 2022. The review included RCTs that compared fluvoxamine plus standard care (or no intervention) to standard care alone (with or without placebo) or to other pharmacological treatments with proven efficacy. The studies included participants with confirmed COVID-19, regardless of disease severity, in both inpatient and outpatient settings. Co-interventions were required to be consistent across study arms. Studies comparing fluvoxamine to pharmacological interventions with unproven efficacy were excluded. The risk of bias for primary outcomes was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool for RCTs. The certainty of evidence for primary outcomes, including mortality, clinical deterioration, clinical improvement, quality of life, serious adverse events, adverse events of any grade, and suicide or suicide attempts, was evaluated using the GRADE approach. Two completed studies involving a total of 1,649 symptomatic participants were identified. One study, conducted in the United States, included 152 participants (80 in the fluvoxamine arm and 72 in the placebo arm). The other study, conducted in Brazil, included 1,497 high-risk participants for progression to severe disease (741 in the fluvoxamine arm and 756 in the placebo arm). Both studies were double-blind, placebo-controlled trials in which participants received 100 mg of fluvoxamine two or three times daily for up to 15 days. Additionally, five ongoing studies and two studies awaiting classification (due to translation issues or missing published data) were identified. No published studies compared fluvoxamine to other pharmacological treatments with proven efficacy. Both included studies were assessed as having a high overall risk of bias. No completed studies were identified that evaluated the use of fluvoxamine in hospitalized COVID-19 patients. For outpatients with mild COVID-19, fluvoxamine in addition to standard care may slightly reduce all-cause mortality at 28 days (relative risk [RR] 0.69, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.38 to 1.27; risk difference [RD] 9 per 1,000; 2 studies, 1,649 participants; low-certainty evidence). Fluvoxamine may also reduce clinical deterioration, defined as all-cause hospital admission or death prior to hospital admission (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.16 to 1.89; RD 57 per 1,000; 2 studies, 1,649 participants; low-certainty evidence). However, there is significant uncertainty regarding the effect of fluvoxamine on serious adverse events (RR 0.56, 95% CI 0.15 to 2.03; RD 54 per 1,000; 2 studies, 1,649 participants; very low-certainty evidence) or adverse events of any grade (RR 1.06, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.37; RD 7 per 1,000; 2 studies, 1,649 participants; very low-certainty evidence). Neither study reported data on symptom resolution (clinical improvement), quality of life, or suicide/suicide attempts. In conclusion, based on low-certainty evidence, fluvoxamine may slightly reduce all-cause mortality at 28 days and may reduce the risk of hospital admission or death in outpatients with mild COVID-19. However, there is considerable uncertainty regarding its effects on serious adverse events or adverse events of any grade. This review will continue to be updated as new eligible trials become available to address gaps in the evidence.
